title: LLM Stack Conversion Playbook — Redwood Demo
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Quasar through a migration playbook to move model calls from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood API. Focus areas: API parity (endpoints, streaming, function-calls), token accounting differences, embedding migration, console mapping, batching/Optimize suggestions, networking (VPC), and security controls. Next steps: run a 48-hour benchmark, share pricing sheet, security pack, and a sample mapping script for prompts and response parsing.
topics: API parity mapping (requests/responses, streaming, stop tokens, function calls)
Embeddings table migration and dimensional/normalization differences
Cost/latency implications and Redwood Optimize suggestions
Console walkthrough: model catalog, routing, rollouts
Private deployment options: VPC connectors and KMS
next_steps: Redwood to provide mapping script and example SDK calls (Priya) — due 2025-10-09
Quasar to provide 3 representative prompts and an eval script (Marta) — due 2025-10-10
Run 48-hour parity benchmark and share results (Evan/Jamal) — kickoff 2025-10-13
Send security pack and SOC2 summary (Jamal) — 2025-10-08

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-07 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~54m | Attendees: Jamal (Redwood AE), Priya (SE), Evan (Product), Marta (Quasar Head of ML), Ravi (Platform), Leah (Security), Tom (PM)

00:00 Jamal: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call. We only have 54 minutes, so we'll do a short intro, then Priya will walk through the migration playbook and a live demo of the API/Console/Optimize features. After that we'll capture next steps.
00:12 Marta: Hi all, Marta here. Excited — we've been looking at moving from OpenAI/Anthropic and a couple of Together models into something we can run more predictably.
00:18 Ravi: Ravi here, will be focused on networking and deployment constraints.
00:22 Leah: Leah - security and compliance.
00:25 Tom: Tom, product. Quick question on scope: we mainly use gpt-style chat, embeddings for semantic search, and a reranker service.
00:34 Jamal: Great, that matches our agenda. Priya, you want to take it?
00:38 Priya: Yep. All right, slide 1 — (note: deck shared: https://redwood.app/decks/ql-llm-conversion.pdf). High-level playbook: 1) parity mapping, 2) eval & benchmark, 3) rollout + routing, 4) cost ops and Optimize tuning. Parity mapping is the tricky bit — request/response shapes are slightly different between OpenAI/Anthropic/Together and Redwood.
01:05 Marta: Can you define parity for us? Is it behavioral parity or API shape parity?
01:11 Priya: Both. For a migration we map the request/response shape so your existing service code needs minimal changes, but we also check behavioral parity — same prompts, same evaluation metrics (ROUGE/BLEU/QA F1, depending). For function-calls there are minor differences in how we encode arguments and how streaming deltas are delivered.
01:28 Jamal: Quick example: OpenAI chat completions send deltas in a stream with role/content chunks; Anthropic has a slightly different role tokenization and Together sometimes bundles meta in the first token. On Redwood our streaming mirrors the OpenAI-style delta structure but we surface an explicit "chunk_index" in the SDK for easier reconciling.
01:50 Tom: Does that mean we need to change our streaming consumer? We rely on partial outputs to show incremental suggestions in UI.
01:56 Priya: Minimal changes. We have an adapter pattern in the mapping script that we will share — basically we translate incoming deltas into your existing UI events. There are a couple of edge cases: stop token handling and multi-function-call edge situations.
02:12 Marta: Embeddings are also a concern — we use OpenAI embeddings for similarity search and we store vectors in Pinecone. Are dimensionalities different?
02:20 Priya: Good question. Most open models have 1k to 2k dims depending on the model; Redwood's curated catalog includes models with explicit dimensions in the model metadata. The main differences are normalization (some providers return L2-normalized vectors, others don't) and tokenization for trimmed prompt-based embeddings. Our Optimize tool suggests whether you should re-normalize or reindex.
02:40 Ravi: Will we have to reindex the entire vector DB? That's expensive.
02:44 Priya: Not always. There are two strategies: 1) on-the-fly re-normalization at query time (cheaper but adds CPU at query), or 2) one-time reindex with batch transforms. We recommend sampling and measuring recall delta first. For Quasar, since you have ~30M vectors, we suggest the sample + reindex if recall drops more than 2-3%.
03:05 Leah: Security — where do logs and tokens live? We need SOC2 controls and KMS integration.
03:11 Jamal: Redwood Hosted stores audit logs in a customer-segregated bucket, logs are encrypted at rest and in transit. For Private deployments we offer a control plane that can be deployed inside your VPC and you can attach your KMS/HSM for key management. I'll send the SOC2/ISO summary and DPA after the call.
03:32 Leah: We also need SSO (SAML) and RBAC.
03:35 Priya: Both are supported in the Console. We'll demo the RBAC screen.
03:39 Jamal: Quick live demo? Priya will do a short mapping example from an OpenAI chat request to Redwood's chat.create endpoint.
03:46 Priya: Okay sharing my screen now — typing an example request:
03:53 Priya (screen): OpenAI-style: POST /v1/chat/completions with messages = [{role: "user", content: "Summarize..."}, ...], temperature = 0.2, max_tokens = 256. On Redwood we have POST /v1/responses with input = {type: "chat", content: ...}, model = "rw-open-1" and we pass options: {stream: true, function_call: {name: ...}}. The mapping script converts messages -> input array and preserves role metadata.
04:25 Tom: How about response ids and token accounting? Our billing logic depends on prompt vs completion tokens.
04:31 Priya: Redwood's response object includes token_usage.prompt_tokens and token_usage.completion_tokens, we mimic OpenAI's fields to keep billing parity. Minor off-by-one differences can occur because of tokenizer differences across models; Optimize will show per-model token deltas in the Console.
04:52 Marta: Together models we use have some different stop token semantics; we've seen hallucinations when truncation differs.
04:58 Priya: We recommend normalizing stop sequences client-side and using explicit max_new_tokens instead of max_tokens when possible. In the mapping script we include a stop-token normalizer.
05:12 Ravi: Networking question — we want Redwood Private behind our VPC with strict egress. What are the connection patterns?
05:19 Jamal: For Private, we support VPC peering and a connector that runs in your environment. Control plane can be out-of-band if you want managed; for air-gapped we have an on-prem package. We'll attach the peer IP ranges and a sample Terraform snippet.
05:36 Evan: Quick note: for Dedicated vs Hosted, think of Dedicated as reserved GPU pools — it's more predictable for latency-sensitive rerankers. We can show a throughput vs cost chart in Optimize.
05:47 Tom: Re: reranker — we currently have a lightweight ranker hosted on CPU; would you recommend moving to a small GPU instance?
05:54 Priya: For rerankers with low-latency SLOs, a quantized GPU model often gives best latency/cost. Optimize suggests quantization profiles per model and can recommend batching thresholds.
06:10 Marta: Can we see the Console routing controls? We often want traffic split between Anthropic and Redwood during a canary.
06:17 Priya (screen): Console -> Routes -> Add route. You can define policy: percent traffic to Redwood-hosted rw-open-1, fallback to Anthropic if latency > 400ms or errorRate > 1%. We support A/B, canary, and model fallbacks. You can pin a user or token to a route.
06:38 Marta: Nice, that helps for gradual migration.
06:41 Tom: Auditing — will we have per-request trace id to join with our logs?
06:44 Jamal: Yes, we emit request_id and trace_id headers. The Console also surfaces per-request token/cost breakdown and you can export logs to Splunk/Datadog.
06:59 Leah: A question about data retention — do hosted logs retain raw user content? We need controls to redact PII and configure retention windows.
07:06 Priya: You can configure retention windows per-organization and enable automatic redaction rules. For private deployments you control the retention entirely.
07:17 Marta: Let's talk about the actual parity metrics. We run a QA test suite and compare F1 and hallucination rates. How do you compare across different model families?
07:25 Priya: We run side-by-side evals using the same prompts and scoring harness. The Console's evals module will show per-prompt deltas and aggregate metrics. For different model families we create normalization layers and post-process to align outputs — e.g., convert tokenization, whitespace, and punctuation normalization so scoring is stable.
07:48 Tom: Do you have an example mapping script we can use to start?
07:52 Priya: Yes — sample repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/migration-scripts. It includes Python adapters for OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood and a small test harness. I'll drop the direct link in the follow-up.
08:06 Marta: Great. For embeddings, can you show how Optimize recommends quantization vs full-precision?
08:12 Priya (screen): Optimize -> Cost Profiles -> Select embedding workload. The tool analyzes request rate and vector size and suggests 8-bit quantization for CPU-heavy workloads or 16-bit on GPU. It also simulates recall delta with a sample dataset. Here's an example: for your 384-dim vectors, reindex + 8-bit compression estimated 12% cost savings with <1.5% recall loss on our sample.
08:45 Ravi: That simulation is helpful. We'll need reproducible numbers for procurement.
08:48 Jamal: Procurement-wise we'll send a pricing sheet with committed and on-demand rates. Dedicated reserved capacity has a different pricing model.
08:56 Tom: On the topic of cost—we're currently getting charged per 1k tokens from OpenAI. How do Redwood rates map?
09:02 Evan: Redwood gives per-token pricing plus per-embedding pricing. For benchmarking we'll run both the same prompt set and measure tokens as reported by Redwood tokenizer to get apples-to-apples. We also surface cost-per-call in the Console.
09:18 Marta: Is there any dev work for function-calling migration? We rely on json-schema returns and deterministic argument ordering.
09:25 Priya: Function-calls on Redwood support JSON schema and deterministic outputs. The main difference: our SDK adds a small wrapper that validates the schema and returns a canonicalized object. That helps reduce downstream parsing errors.
09:42 Tom: Any known gotchas when converting Together outputs?
09:45 Priya: Together sometimes emits combined text + metadata in one chunk; the adapter splits those into structured fields. We also recommend adding a small validation layer in your client to handle malformed responses gracefully.
09:56 Marta: Ok, assume we want a 48-hour parity run. What's included?
10:00 Jamal: We'll do the following: deploy a Redwood endpoint matching the model family, run your 3 representative prompt families at production QPS, collect latency/percentiles, token usage, and quality metrics. We'll also run an embedding recall pass on a sampled index. We'll hand you raw logs and a summary report.
10:22 Ravi: What kind of telemetry do you need from us? Network egress, sample corpus, and a few service keys?
10:28 Jamal: We'll need a service account key to hit the endpoint, sample corpus, and expected QPS. We'll do the benchmark in a sandbox Dedicated pool unless you prefer hosted.
10:37 Leah: Regarding contractual stuff: we need a DPA and an SOC2 attestation. Also, can you confirm data residency options for EU customers?
10:45 Jamal: DPA yes; SOC2 report available. For EU-residency we can pin routing to eu-west-1 regions and for Private deployments you control data locality. We'll include regional routing docs.
10:58 Tom: Anything about latency SLOs? We need p95 < 250ms for rerank calls.
11:03 Priya: For small context and quantized models on Dedicated GPU with optimized kernels, p95 < 200ms is achievable. We'll show the config we used in past customers.
11:12 Marta: Let's surface some of the small differences you mentioned earlier — tokenizer mismatch example?
11:16 Priya: Sure — one example: the sequence prefix when you include system instructions can shift token count by 1-3 tokens across different tokenizers. That makes raw token counts non-identical. Optimize will show per-model delta and propose either prompt rewriting or a small client-side offset.
11:34 Tom: Any reliability concerns with fallback routing between providers? We want no visible error to end users.
11:38 Evan: We support circuit-breaker policies and graceful degradation paths: short-circuit to cached answer, lower-fidelity model, or fallback vendor. The routing layer can also do gradual traffic shifts based on latency and error budgets.
11:52 Marta: Okay, final recap?
11:55 Jamal: Recap: we'll share mapping script and repo, run a 48-hour parity benchmark, send pricing and security pack, and Priya will provide the specific SDK code snippets. Quasar will provide prompts and a small eval harness.
12:09 Tom: Sounds good. We'll also need a draft runbook for rollback in case of quality regression.
12:14 Jamal: We'll draft a rollback runbook as part of the benchmark deliverable.
12:20 Leah: Thanks everyone. Please share SOC2 docs and DPA ASAP.
12:23 Jamal: Will do. Thanks all.
12:26 (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: speaker labels mostly accurate; occasional mis-hearings (e.g., Together vs "two-gether"). References to shared artifacts: deck link, github migration-scripts repo, and a sample pricing sheet to be sent.
